claim: Mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene are responsible for Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), a genetic predisposition to colorectal cancer.
source: Mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene are responsible for Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), a genetic predisposition to colorectal cancer, and are also found in the majority of sporadic colonic tumors (Fearnhead et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fearnhead et al., 2001

claim: APC mutations are found in the majority of sporadic colonic tumors.
source: Mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene are responsible for Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP), a genetic predisposition to colorectal cancer, and are also found in the majority of sporadic colonic tumors (Fearnhead et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fearnhead et al., 2001

claim: APC negatively regulates the proliferative consequences of Wnt signaling through degradation of β-catenin.
source: Critical roles for APC in colon carcinogenesis are attributed to its ability to negatively regulate the proliferative consequences of Wnt signaling through degradation of β-catenin, and maintain normal intestinal differentiation by controlling the biosynthesis of retinoic acid (RA) (Jette et al., 2004; Nadauld et al., 2006a, 2004, 2005; Rai et al., 2010; Schneikert et al., 2007; Shelton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Jette et al., 2004; Nadauld et al., 2006a, 2004, 2005; Rai et al., 2010; Schneikert et al., 2007; Shelton et al., 2006

claim: APC maintains normal intestinal differentiation by controlling the biosynthesis of retinoic acid (RA).
source: Critical roles for APC in colon carcinogenesis are attributed to its ability to negatively regulate the proliferative consequences of Wnt signaling through degradation of β-catenin, and maintain normal intestinal differentiation by controlling the biosynthesis of retinoic acid (RA) (Jette et al., 2004; Nadauld et al., 2006a, 2004, 2005; Rai et al., 2010; Schneikert et al., 2007; Shelton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Jette et al., 2004; Nadauld et al., 2006a, 2004, 2005; Rai et al., 2010; Schneikert et al., 2007; Shelton et al., 2006

claim: Altered energy metabolism is an emerging hallmark in cancer.
source: Altered energy metabolism is an emerging hallmark in cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011

claim: Cancer cells favor aerobic glycolysis even in the presence of ample oxygen, a phenomenon known as the Warburg effect.
source: The observation that cancer cells produce energy to support cell growth and proliferation differently than normal cells is known as the Warburg effect, and refers to neoplastic cells favoring aerobic glycolysis, even in the presence of ample oxygen (Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Warburg, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vander Heiden et al., 2009 and Warburg, 1956

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction through impaired pyruvate metabolism is one of the major molecular mechanisms contributing to the Warburg effect.
source: One of the major molecular mechanisms contributing to Warburg effect is mitochondrial dysfunction through impaired pyruvate metabolism (Diaz-Ruiz et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diaz-Ruiz et al., 2011

claim: MPC1 is part of the MPC complex that is responsible for the uptake of pyruvate into the inner mitochondrial matrix.
source: The recently identified mitochondrial pyruvate carrier subunit MPC1 is part of the MPC complex that is responsible for the uptake of pyruvate into the inner mitochondrial matrix (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bricker et al., 2012 and Herzig et al., 2012

claim: MPC1 is downregulated in various human cancers and this correlates with poor survival.
source: Recent work has revealed that MPC1 is downregulated in various human cancers and that this correlates with poor survival (Schell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schell et al., 2014

claim: Re-expression of MPC1 repressed the Warburg effect in colon cancer cell lines.
source: Consistent with a causative role in tumorigenesis, re-expression of MPC1 repressed the Warburg effect in colon cancer cell lines (Schell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schell et al., 2014

claim: mpc1 is significantly downregulated in apcmcr embryos compared to WT/het siblings.
source: Evaluating gene expression of mpc1 and mpc2 by qRT-PCR, we found that both genes were significantly downregulated in apcmcr and apc mo embryos compared to WT/het siblings and control mo, respectively (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: mpc2 is significantly downregulated in apcmcr embryos compared to WT/het siblings.
source: Evaluating gene expression of mpc1 and mpc2 by qRT-PCR, we found that both genes were significantly downregulated in apcmcr and apc mo embryos compared to WT/het siblings and control mo, respectively (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: mpc1 is significantly downregulated in apc mo embryos compared to control mo.
source: Evaluating gene expression of mpc1 and mpc2 by qRT-PCR, we found that both genes were significantly downregulated in apcmcr and apc mo embryos compared to WT/het siblings and control mo, respectively (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: mpc2 is significantly downregulated in apc mo embryos compared to control mo.
source: Evaluating gene expression of mpc1 and mpc2 by qRT-PCR, we found that both genes were significantly downregulated in apcmcr and apc mo embryos compared to WT/het siblings and control mo, respectively (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: mpc1 and mpc2 are expressed in the head, eyes, vasculature and somites at 24-48 hpf in WT embryos.
source: Additional in situ analyses for mpc1 and mpc2 in WT embryos revealed staining in the head, eyes, vasculature and somites at 24–48 hr post-fertilization (hpf) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E

claim: mpc1 and mpc2 expression in the pectoral fin buds, liver and gut emerges at later time points in WT embryos.
source: At later time points, expression in the pectoral fin buds, liver and gut emerged (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E

claim: mpc1 and mpc2 are expressed in the gut of 72 hpf WT embryos.
source: Cross sections of 72 hpf WT embryos previously probed with mpc1 and mpc2 confirmed gut expression for both genes (black arrows) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by cross-section data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Microinjection of 0.75 mM mpc1 morpholino into WT embryos resulted in about 87% of injected embryos appearing morphant.
source: Microinjection of 0.75 mM mpc1 morpholino into WT embryos at the one- to two-cell stage resulted in about 87% of injected embryos appearing morphant (n = 228) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by morpholino injection data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: mpc1 morphants exhibited smaller head and eyes, enlarged hindbrain vesicle, pericardial edema, body curvature, and loss of pectoral fins.
source: Consistent with downregulation of mpc1 in apcmcr, mpc1 morphants (mpc1 mo) exhibited a range of phenotypes consisting of smaller head and eyes, enlarged hindbrain vesicle (black arrows), pericardial edema, body curvature, and loss of pectoral fins (blue arrows) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 2A

claim: The primordial gut formed in 93% of mpc1 mo embryos.
source: In situ hybridization with gata6 revealed that the primordial gut formed (93%, n = 55) in mpc1 mo but developed abnormally, as shown by reduced staining for fabp2 (100%, n = 36), which marks the differentiated gut (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The gut developed abnormally in mpc1 mo embryos as shown by reduced staining for fabp2.
source: In situ hybridization with gata6 revealed that the primordial gut formed (93%, n = 55) in mpc1 mo but developed abnormally, as shown by reduced staining for fabp2 (100%, n = 36), which marks the differentiated gut (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: mpc1 mo gut had fewer cells comprising the gut tube and they appeared cuboidal and non-polarized.
source: Histological analyses on mpc1 mo gut confirmed these findings, there were fewer cells comprising the gut tube and they appeared cuboidal and non-polarized (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Intestinal folds were visibly lacking in the mpc1 mo gut.
source: Additionally, intestinal folds were visibly lacking in the mpc1 mo gut (black arrow, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2C

claim: irbp, a marker for photoreceptor and retinal pigmented epithelial cells, was severely reduced in 95% of mpc1 mo embryos.
source: Since APC has also been reported to play a crucial role in congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) in humans and normal ocular development in the zebrafish embryo, we examined the eyes of mpc1 mo and found that irbp, a marker for photoreceptor and retinal pigmented epithelial cells, was severely reduced in mpc1 mo (95%, n = 40) (Figure 2B) (Nadauld et al., 2006b; Chapman et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B and citations to Nadauld et al., 2006b and Chapman et al., 1989

claim: mpc1 mo eyes had small lens and disorganized cell layers.
source: Cross-section of mpc1 mo eye revealed small lens and disorganized cell layers (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 2C

claim: mpc1 mo showed diminished maturation for brain as indicated by ascl1a expression in 95% of embryos.
source: Further phenotypic analyses of mpc1 mo by in situ hybridization using tissue-specific markers exposed diminished maturation for brain (95%, n = 22) and fin buds (100%, n = 28) as indicated by ascl1a and id1 expression, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: mpc1 mo showed diminished maturation for fin buds as indicated by id1 expression in 100% of embryos.
source: Further phenotypic analyses of mpc1 mo by in situ hybridization using tissue-specific markers exposed diminished maturation for brain (95%, n = 22) and fin buds (100%, n = 28) as indicated by ascl1a and id1 expression, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: mpc1 mo hearts failed to loop as determined by myl7 staining in 100% of embryos.
source: Also, mpc1 mo hearts failed to loop as determined by myl7 staining (100%, n = 39) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Terminal differentiation of the pancreas in mpc1 mo was severely reduced as assessed by trypsin expression in 100% of embryos.
source: As with the gut, terminal differentiation of the pancreas in mpc1 mo was severely reduced as assessed by trypsin expression, a marker for exocrine pancreas (100%, n = 28) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Insulin expression, denoting the endocrine pancreas, remained normal in 100% of mpc1 mo embryos.
source: Insulin, denoting the endocrine pancreas, remained normal (100%, n = 25) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Alcian blue staining confirmed the absence of pectoral fins and revealed improper jaw formation in 100% of mpc1 mo embryos.
source: Cartilage staining with alcian blue confirmed the absence of pectoral fins and revealed improper jaw formation in mpc1 mo (100%, n = 152) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by alcian blue staining data shown in Figure 2B

claim: MPC1 mRNA restored fin development in 50% of mpc1 mo embryos as indicated by id1 staining.
source: However, in co-injected embryos (mpc1 mo + MPC1 RNA), we found that MPC1 mRNA restored fin development as indicated by id1 staining (50%, n = 49) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: MPC1 mRNA was able to rescue normal midbrain and eye development in mpc1 mo.
source: We obtained similar results with otx2, MPC1 mRNA was able to rescue normal midbrain and eye development in mpc1 mo (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: mpc2 morphants exhibited similar developmental defects as mpc1 morphants, such as smaller head and eyes, enlarged hindbrain vesicle, body curvature, and absence of pectoral fins.
source: We found that mpc2 mo exhibited similar developmental defects as mpc1 mo, such as smaller head and eyes, enlarged hindbrain vesicle (black arrows), body curvature, and absence of pectoral fins (blue arrows) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Only a third of mpc2 mo-injected embryos appeared morphant, the majority of which exhibited a mild phenotype.
source: In contrast to mpc1 mo, only a third of mpc2 mo-injected embryos appeared morphant, the majority of which exhibited a mild phenotype (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by morpholino injection data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: There was a significant increase in embryos with differentiated gut in the apc mo + MPC1 RNA group (29%, n = 312) compared to apc mo alone (6%, n = 265).
source: Compared to apc mo (6%, n = 265), there was a significant increase in embryos with differentiated gut in the morpholino plus mRNA group (29%, n = 312) (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A,C

claim: 40% of apcmcr embryos injected with MPC1 mRNA re-expressed fabp2.
source: We confirmed this finding by injecting 0.5 ng MPC1 mRNA into apcmcr and observed similar results, 40% of injected embryos re-expressed fabp2 (n = 52) (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B,D

claim: Only 3% of un-injected apcmcr showed fabp2 staining.
source: However, only 3% of un-injected apcmcr showed fabp2 staining (n = 29), while WT/het siblings were all positive (n = 80, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data

claim: MPC1 was able to rescue cardiac defects in apcmcr, as improved blood circulation was observed in injected mutants.
source: MPC1 was also able to rescue cardiac defects in apcmcr, as we saw improved blood circulation in injected mutants as well (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by observational data

claim: There was a significant reduction in oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in mpc1 mo compared to control.
source: We assessed mitochondrial respiration by measuring oxidative consumption rates (OCR) in 72 hpf embryos and there was a significant reduction in OCR in mpc1 mo compared to control (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by OCR measurement data shown in Figure 4A

claim: There was an extensive dysregulation of pyruvate metabolism upon loss of mpc1, with a profound upregulation of pyruvate metabolic genes in mpc1 mo.
source: Moreover, there was an extensive dysregulation of pyruvate metabolism upon loss of mpc1, as we discovered a profound upregulation of pyruvate metabolic genes in mpc1 mo, suggesting a compensatory mechanism to account for reduced pyruvate transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Knock down of mpc2 did not affect mpc1 transcript level.
source: Knock down of mpc2 did not affect mpc1 transcript level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: apcmcr and apc mo exhibited significant defects in mitochondrial function compared to appropriate controls.
source: To test this, we evaluated mitochondrial respiration and TG levels in apcmcr and apc mo and compared to appropriate controls, we observed significant defects in mitochondrial function upon loss of apc (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by OCR and TG measurement data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Several enzymes in the pyruvate pathway were differentially regulated in apcmcr or apc mo.
source: Several enzymes in the pyruvate pathway were also differentially regulated in apcmcr or apc mo (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: apcmcr embryos overexpressing MPC1 showed a significant reduction in lactate compared to un-injected apcmcr.
source: Compared to un-injected apcmcr, mutant embryos overexpressing MPC1 showed a significant reduction in lactate (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by lactate measurement data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Loss of pcxb resulted in only 22% of embryos with phenotype.
source: Interestingly, knock down of pcxb resulted in only 22% of embryos with phenotype (n = 27) while targeting pdha1a gave a higher percentage of morphant embryos (63%, n = 19) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by morpholino injection data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: Targeting pdha1a gave a higher percentage of morphant embryos (63%).
source: Interestingly, knock down of pcxb resulted in only 22% of embryos with phenotype (n = 27) while targeting pdha1a gave a higher percentage of morphant embryos (63%, n = 19) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by morpholino injection data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: A synergistic effect was observed when both pcxb and pdha1a were diminished (83%).
source: A synergistic effect was observed when both enzymes were diminished (83%, n = 18) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by morpholino injection data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: fabp2 in situ staining revealed intestinal developmental defects in the pdha1a mo, pcxb mo and pdha1a + pcxb morphant embryos.
source: fabp2 in situ staining (black arrows) also revealed intestinal developmental defects in the pdha1a mo, pcxb mo and pdha1a + pcxb morphant embryos (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4H

claim: Treatment of apc mo with 10 uM NS-398 did not affect mpc1 or mpc2 levels.
source: Perturbation of the Wnt pathway by treatment of apc mo with 10 uM NS-398, a COX-2-specific inhibitor that has been shown to impair β-catenin activity in an apc-deficient background, did not affect mpc1 or mpc2 levels (Figure 5A) (Eisinger et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Eisinger et al., 2007

claim: Treatment of apc mo with 10 uM NS-398 resulted in a dramatic reduction in expression of mmp9.
source: We did see a dramatic reduction in expression of known β-catenin target gene, mmp9, implying that apc regulation of mpc1 is independent of Wnt (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: apc regulation of mpc1 is independent of Wnt signaling.
source: We did see a dramatic reduction in expression of known β-catenin target gene, mmp9, implying that apc regulation of mpc1 is independent of Wnt (Figure 5A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NS-398 treatment reduced mmp9 but not mpc1/mpc2 levels

claim: mpc1 and mpc2 transcript levels went down significantly with inhibition of RA by DEAB treatment.
source: By qRT-PCR, we found that mpc1 and mpc2 transcript levels went down significantly with inhibition of RA (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Five pyruvate metabolism genes were either up- or downregulated upon DEAB treatment.
source: Expanding our analyses to include other components of pyruvate metabolism, there were five other genes that were either up- or downregulated upon DEAB treatment, supporting the notion that the pyruvate metabolic program is altered at various points when RA levels are perturbed (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: DEAB-treated embryos had low lactate levels.
source: The DEAB-treated embryos also had low lactate levels, further establishing that RA inhibition results in mitochondrial dysfunction (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by lactate measurement data shown in Figure 5D

claim: MPC1 expression is significantly downregulated in colon adenocarcinomas with APC deletions compared to normal colon.
source: Consistent with our previous data, we found that mpc1 expression is significantly downregulated in colon adenocarcinomas with APC deletions (n = 91) compared to normal colon (n = 19) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: MPC1, MPC2, PDHA1 and PC showed consistent downregulation in colon mucinous adenocarcinomas.
source: We also looked at other genes involved in pyruvate transport and metabolism and interestingly, MPC1, MPC2, PDHA1 and PC showed consistent downregulation in a specific subset of colon adenocarcinomas known as colon mucinous adenocarcinomas (AC) (n = 22) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: There were five colorectal cancer samples in COSMIC with somatic APC deletions that had mutations in multiple pyruvate metabolism enzymes.
source: There were five samples with somatic APC deletions that had mutations in multiple pyruvate metabolism enzymes as well, most of which are predicted to be probably (**) or possibly (*) damaging, further supporting a genetic link between APC mutation and dysregulation of pyruvate metabolism (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by COSMIC database analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: The pyruvate metabolism pathway is significantly dysregulated in cancer compared to a group of randomly-generated Uniprot genes.
source: Using Oncomine, we extended these studies by treating the genes involved in pyruvate transport and metabolism as a group (n = 10). We discovered that this pathway is significantly dysregulated in cancer compared to a group of randomly-generated Uniprot genes (n = 55) (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by Oncomine database analysis shown in Figure 6B and Supplementary file 1

claim: Only colorectal adenocarcinoma and kidney chromophobe carcinoma showed a significant difference in overall survival between patients with or without mutations and/or gene expression changes in the pyruvate metabolism gene set.
source: Out of 21 cancer types that we analyzed, only colorectal adenocarcinoma and kidney chromophobe carcinoma showed a significant difference in overall survival between the two groups (Figure 6C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by cBioportal analysis shown in Figure 6C and Supplementary file 2

claim: apc controls the levels of mpc1.
source: Utilizing zebrafish to examine the genetic relationship between MPC1 and Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC), a key tumor suppressor in colorectal cancer, we found that apc controls the levels of mpc1 and that knock down of mpc1 recapitulates phenotypes of impaired apc function including failed intestinal differentiation.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization data showing mpc1 downregulation in apc-deficient embryos

claim: Knock down of mpc1 recapitulates phenotypes of impaired apc function including failed intestinal differentiation.
source: Utilizing zebrafish to examine the genetic relationship between MPC1 and Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC), a key tumor suppressor in colorectal cancer, we found that apc controls the levels of mpc1 and that knock down of mpc1 recapitulates phenotypes of impaired apc function including failed intestinal differentiation.
evidence: Supported by morphological and molecular analyses of mpc1 morphants

claim: Exogenous human MPC1 RNA rescued failed intestinal differentiation in zebrafish models of apc deficiency.
source: Exogenous human MPC1 RNA rescued failed intestinal differentiation in zebrafish models of apc deficiency.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing increased fabp2 expression in apc-deficient embryos injected with MPC1 RNA

claim: apc has a novel role in pyruvate metabolism.
source: Our data demonstrate a novel role for apc in pyruvate metabolism and that pyruvate metabolism dictates intestinal cell fate and differentiation decisions downstream of apc.
evidence: Supported by data showing apc regulation of mpc1 and pyruvate metabolism genes

claim: Pyruvate metabolism dictates intestinal cell fate and differentiation decisions downstream of apc.
source: Our data demonstrate a novel role for apc in pyruvate metabolism and that pyruvate metabolism dictates intestinal cell fate and differentiation decisions downstream of apc.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing MPC1 can restore intestinal differentiation in apc-deficient embryos

claim: The apcmcr zebrafish is homozygous for a truncating mutation in the Mutation Cluster Region (MCR) of apc similar to what is found in human colon tumors.
source: To investigate the relationship between apc and mpc, we utilized the apcmcr zebrafish, which is homozygous for a truncating mutation in the Mutation Cluster Region (MCR) of apc and similar to what is found in human colon tumors (Hurlstone et al., 2003; Miyoshi et al., 1992a, 1992b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurlstone et al., 2003 and Miyoshi et al., 1992a, 1992b

claim: mpc1 and mpc2 form a heterodimer complex that is responsible for transporting pyruvate from the inner mitochondrial space into the inner mitochondrial matrix.
source: mpc1 and mpc2 form a heterodimer complex that is responsible for transporting pyruvate from the inner mitochondrial space into the inner mitochondrial matrix (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bricker et al., 2012 and Herzig et al., 2012

claim: MPC2 expression is inconsistently altered in cancer and variably correlated with survival.
source: MPC2 expression is inconsistently altered in cancer and variably correlated with survival (Schell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schell et al., 2014

claim: APC has been reported to play a crucial role in congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) in humans and normal ocular development in the zebrafish embryo.
source: Since APC has also been reported to play a crucial role in congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) in humans and normal ocular development in the zebrafish embryo, we examined the eyes of mpc1 mo and found that irbp, a marker for photoreceptor and retinal pigmented epithelial cells, was severely reduced in mpc1 mo (95%, n = 40) (Figure 2B) (Nadauld et al., 2006b; Chapman et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nadauld et al., 2006b and Chapman et al., 1989

claim: Overexpression of MPC1 mRNA alone resulted mostly in normal-appearing embryos, with a small percentage exhibiting cyclopia, severe body curvature and truncated tail (29%).
source: Overexpression of MPC1 mRNA alone resulted mostly in normal-appearing embryos, a small percentage exhibited cyclopia, severe body curvature and truncated tail (29%, n = 187) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Pyruvate can be transported into the mitochondria and used to drive ATP production and generate building blocks for macromolecule biosynthesis through oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Contingent on the metabolic needs of the cell, pyruvate can be transported into the mitochondria, and through the action mainly of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), it can be used to drive ATP production and generate building blocks for macromolecule biosynthesis through oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of pyruvate metabolism

claim: Pyruvate can be converted to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and exported out of the cell.
source: Alternatively, pyruvate can be converted to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and exported out of the cell.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of pyruvate metabolism

claim: Aberrations in genes involved in pyruvate metabolism and transport have been reported in human diseases, particularly in cancer.
source: Aberrations in genes involved in pyruvate metabolism and transport have been reported in human diseases, particularly in cancer (Gray et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gray et al., 2014

claim: Monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4) and LDHA are overexpressed in cancer.
source: For example, monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4) and LDHA are overexpressed in cancer (Kim et al., 2013; Rong et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013 and Rong et al., 2013

claim: An isoform of pyruvate kinase 2 (PKM2) is preferentially expressed in numerous cancer types including pancreatic, colon and lung.
source: An isoform of pyruvate kinase 2 (PKM2) is preferentially expressed in numerous cancer types including pancreatic, colon and lung, and has been shown to promote aerobic glycolysis in HeLa cells by functioning as a transcriptional coactivator for HIF-1 (Cerwenka et al., 1999; Christofk et al., 2008; Luo and Semenza, 2011; Schneider et al., 2002; Yeh et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cerwenka et al., 1999; Christofk et al., 2008; Luo and Semenza, 2011; Schneider et al., 2002; Yeh et al., 2008

claim: PKM2 has been shown to promote aerobic glycolysis in HeLa cells by functioning as a transcriptional coactivator for HIF-1.
source: An isoform of pyruvate kinase 2 (PKM2) is preferentially expressed in numerous cancer types including pancreatic, colon and lung, and has been shown to promote aerobic glycolysis in HeLa cells by functioning as a transcriptional coactivator for HIF-1 (Cerwenka et al., 1999; Christofk et al., 2008; Luo and Semenza, 2011; Schneider et al., 2002; Yeh et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cerwenka et al., 1999; Christofk et al., 2008; Luo and Semenza, 2011; Schneider et al., 2002; Yeh et al., 2008

claim: Restoration of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity through inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 1 (PDK1) in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cell lines led to reduced HIF-1a expression and tumor growth.
source: Restoration of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex activity through inhibition of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 1 (PDK1) in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma cell lines led to reduced HIF-1a expression and tumor growth (McFate et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to McFate et al., 2008

claim: The upregulation of pyruvate metabolic genes in mpc1 mo suggests a compensatory mechanism to account for reduced pyruvate transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: Moreover, there was an extensive dysregulation of pyruvate metabolism upon loss of mpc1, as we discovered a profound upregulation of pyruvate metabolic genes in mpc1 mo, suggesting a compensatory mechanism to account for reduced pyruvate transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of upregulated pyruvate metabolic genes in mpc1 morphants

claim: APC positively regulates glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) activity, an enzyme that inhibits glycogen synthase (GS) which is involved in converting glucose into glycogen for storage.
source: APC has been shown to positively regulate glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) activity, an enzyme that inhibits glycogen synthase (GS) which is involved in converting glucose into glycogen for storage (Bouskila et al., 2010; Valvezan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouskila et al., 2010 and Valvezan et al., 2012

claim: APC plays a major role in controlling cellular bioenergetics and homeostasis, as it can affect glycogen synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation through GSK-3 and MPC1, respectively.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest a major role for APC in controlling cellular bioenergetics and homeostasis, as it can affect glycogen synthesis and oxidative phosphorylation through GSK-3 and MPC1, respectively.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings about APC regulation of GSK-3 and MPC1

claim: The rescue of intestinal differentiation defects in embryos with impaired apc function by exogenous MPC1 mRNA establishes a clear role for metabolic programming as a switch that can control cell fate decisions.
source: The rescue of intestinal differentiation defects in embryos with impaired apc function by exogenous MPC1 mRNA establishes a clear role for metabolic programming as a switch that can control cell fate decisions (Figure 3).
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing MPC1 can restore intestinal differentiation

claim: RA may control a program of metabolism that is permissive for intestinal differentiation.
source: In this respect, the role of retinoic acid in promoting cell fate and differentiation remains undefined. Our studies suggest that RA may control a program of metabolism that is permissive for intestinal differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RA inhibition affects pyruvate metabolism genes

claim: The effects of RA on metabolism are likely indirect.
source: The actions of RA are complex, and it is likely that the effects of RA on metabolism are indirect.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the complexity of RA actions

claim: Treatment of either WT or apcmcr embryos with RA did not result in an immediate induction of mpc1.
source: Consistent with this, treatment of either WT or apcmcr embryos with RA did not result in an immediate induction of mpc1 (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Metabolic changes are a major part of the decision process in determining cell fate.
source: Our data strongly support the notion that metabolic changes are a major part of the decision process in determining cell fate and provide a better understanding of how cancer genetics is linked with biochemical metabolic pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study

claim: There is a genetic link between APC mutation and dysregulation of pyruvate metabolism.
source: There were five samples with somatic APC deletions that had mutations in multiple pyruvate metabolism enzymes as well, most of which are predicted to be probably (**) or possibly (*) damaging, further supporting a genetic link between APC mutation and dysregulation of pyruvate metabolism (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by COSMIC database analysis showing co-occurrence of APC and pyruvate metabolism gene mutations

claim: Pyruvate metabolism genes have potential use as prognostic markers for colorectal adenocarcinoma and kidney chromophobe carcinoma.
source: Out of 21 cancer types that we analyzed, only colorectal adenocarcinoma and kidney chromophobe carcinoma showed a significant difference in overall survival between the two groups (Figure 6C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between pyruvate metabolism gene alterations and overall survival in these cancer types

claim: Loss of MPC1, MPC2, PDHA1 and PC essentially shuts down oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria.
source: It is remarkable how MPC1 and MPC2, PDHA1 and PC—genes that are involved in the transport and conversion of pyruvate in the inner mitochondrial matrix, respectively—are all significantly downregulated in a subset of colon adenocarcinomas categorized as colon mucinous adenocarcinomas, as loss of these genes essentially shuts down oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on knowledge of the roles of these genes in pyruvate metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation

claim: Regulation of other metabolic genes by APC could occur in parallel with regulation of mpc1.
source: In addition, regulation of other metabolic genes by APC could occur in parallel with regulation of mpc1.
evidence: Speculative reasoning to explain differences in pyruvate metabolism gene dysregulation between apc and mpc1 knockdown

claim: Knock down of pcxb expression resulted in low penetrance and mild phenotype.
source: Knock down of pcxb expression, however, not only resulted in low penetrance but mild phenotype as well (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 4F-H

claim: The low penetrance and mild phenotype of pcxb knockdown could be due to the activation of an alternative pathway where oxaloacetate can be derived from glutamine instead of pyruvate.
source: This could be due to the activation of an alternative pathway where oxaloacetate can be derived from glutamine instead of pyruvate (DeBerardinis et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citation to DeBerardinis et al., 2007

claim: NS-398 is a COX-2-specific inhibitor that has been shown to impair β-catenin activity in an apc-deficient background.
source: Perturbation of the Wnt pathway by treatment of apc mo with 10 uM NS-398, a COX-2-specific inhibitor that has been shown to impair β-catenin activity in an apc-deficient background, did not affect mpc1 or mpc2 levels (Figure 5A) (Eisinger et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eisinger et al., 2007

claim: DEAB is a known inhibitor of RALDH which catalyzes the second step in the conversion of Vitamin A to the active metabolite, RA.
source: To interrogate the involvement of RA in pyruvate metabolism downstream of apc, we treated WT embryos with DMSO or 5 uM DEAB, a known inhibitor of RALDH which catalyzes the second step in the conversion of Vitamin A to the active metabolite, RA (Marill et al., 2003; Russo et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marill et al., 2003 and Russo et al., 1988

claim: The pyruvate metabolic program is altered at various points when RA levels are perturbed.
source: Expanding our analyses to include other components of pyruvate metabolism, there were five other genes that were either up- or downregulated upon DEAB treatment, supporting the notion that the pyruvate metabolic program is altered at various points when RA levels are perturbed (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing multiple pyruvate metabolism genes affected by DEAB treatment

claim: RA inhibition results in mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: The DEAB-treated embryos also had low lactate levels, further establishing that RA inhibition results in mitochondrial dysfunction (Figure 5D).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of low lactate levels in DEAB-treated embryos
